messages.subject: questions about targeted sequencing results
parts:
Hi,

I'm new to CNV analysis, and am trying to use Codex to analyze germline copy number variation in a targeted sequencing experiment looking at ~1000 genes or small intergenic regions. Most of the genes are OR genes, which are known to have a lot of variation in copy number. My sample includes 150 individuals from six populations. I have been following the code posted on Github for targeted sequencing. I have one quick question and then a more involved question--

1. Is the following set of commands in targeted sequencing one you recommend for general use for further QC of samples or is that just for the example dataset?
sampfilter=apply(Y_qc,2,median)>=50   # need to exclude 3 samples (exon capture failure)
sampname_qc=sampname_qc[sampfilter]
Y_qc=Y_qc[,sampfilter]

2. I am able to get the program to run successfully, but I'm having trouble with the segmentation step. When I source the 'segment_targeted.R' script and run the For loop to make the finalcall file, the finalcall file ends up being one row of NA (see below). Does that mean the program is finding no copy number variation in my data? The optimal K is estimated at 13, but I get the same result if I make K lower (such as K=2). 

> dim(Y_qc)
[1] 809 121
> length(ref_qc)
[1] 809
> length(sampname_qc)
[1] 121
> dim(Yhat[[2]])
[1] 809 121
> length(chr_qc)
[1] 809
> optK=2
> finalcall=matrix(ncol=14)
> colnames(finalcall)=c('sample_name','chr','gene','cnv',
+                       'st_bp','ed_bp','length_kb',
+                       'st_exon','ed_exon','raw_cov',
+                       'norm_cov','copy_no','lratio',
+                       'mBIC')
> for(genei in unique(gene_qc)){
+ cat('Segmenting gene',genei,'\n')
+ geneindex=which(gene_qc==genei)
+ yi=Y_qc[geneindex,]
+ yhati=Yhat[[optK]][geneindex,]
+ refi=ref_qc[geneindex]
+ chri=chr_qc[geneindex][1]
+ finalcalli=segment_targeted(yi, yhati, sampname_qc, refi, genei, chri, lmax=length(geneindex), mode='integer')
+ finalcall=rbind(finalcall,finalcalli)
+ }
Segmenting gene OR4G4P 
Segmenting gene OR4G11P 
...
Segmenting gene OR2AF1P 
Segmenting gene OR3B1P 
> finalcall
     sample_name chr gene cnv st_bp ed_bp length_kb st_exon ed_exon raw_cov
[1,] NA          NA  NA   NA  NA    NA    NA        NA      NA      NA     
     norm_cov copy_no lratio mBIC
[1,] NA       NA      NA     NA  

I tried using the finalcall commands in the Bioconductor vignette instead of the targeted sequencing ones to see what happens (with optK = 13)-
finalcall <- segment(Y_qc, Yhat, optK = optK, K = K, sampname_qc, ref_qc, chr, lmax = 200, mode = "integer")
When I do that, I get around 300 total deletions/duplications across 112 individuals (1-5 deletions/duplications per individual). However, some of the regions seem really long and a few "cross" chromosomes, which I'm guessing is because of the data is from targeted sequencing and not whole exome.

Do you have any suggestions on how I should proceed? Could I be doing something wrong with the segmentation step in the targeted selection protocol? Or is the 0 deletions/duplications result valid?

Thank you very much!
Carrie

This is used for one dataset that I analyzed, which requires the median read depth across all targets for a sample to be greater than 50. Sometimes the library prep failed for certain samples and this QC is used to remove these samples. When I do that, I get around 300 total deletions/duplications across 112 individuals (1-5 deletions/duplications per individual). However, some of the regions seem really long and a few "cross" chromosomes, which I'm guessing is because of the data is from targeted sequencing and not whole exome.

Do you have any suggestions on how I should proceed? Could I be doing something wrong with the segmentation step in the targeted selection protocol? Or is the 0 deletions/duplications result valid?

I think your number of latent factors is chosen to high (opt =13 currently). This will remove most of your CNV signals as latent artifacts or batch effects. You can refer to the pdf generated in the choiceofK() step however it can be sometimes not indicative of an optimal value. If this is the case, I still would recommend a smaller optK — we rarely set this value to be greater than 10 in our analysis (usually around 5). Also for your dataset, it seems that you have some positive controls, which you can use to guide the choice of optK (i.e., try different optK and see if the known CNV signals are retained without too many potential false positives).

Thank you very much!
Carrie

Hi Carrie,

You need to use the segmentation function for targeted sequencing since the targets are very sparse along the genome and segmentation for each chromosome wouldnt make sense. I think there must be something wrong with your code.  Can you try debug by looking into the for loop? This code has been used several times and I feel you might have some trivial misspecification.

for(genei in unique(gene_qc)){
+ cat('Segmenting gene',genei,'\n')
+ geneindex=which(gene_qc==genei)
+ yi=Y_qc[geneindex,]
+ yhati=Yhat[[optK]][geneindex,]
+ refi=ref_qc[geneindex]
+ chri=chr_qc[geneindex][1]
+ finalcalli=segment_targeted(yi, yhati, sampname_qc, refi, genei, chri, lmax=length(geneindex), mode='integer')
+ finalcall=rbind(finalcall,finalcalli)
+ }

If you cannot find it, please use save.image(file=‘codex_debug.rda’) and send me the image rda file (or share with me via Google or Dropbox if it is too large). I can help you look into it.

Cheers,
Yuchao

messages.subject: Re: [codex_wes_cnv] questions about targeted sequencing results
parts:
Hi,

I took a look at your rda file. The error you got was due to the fact that each gene has only 1 target. You have 860 targets after QC, which correspond to 860 genes. The segmentation procedure by segment_targeted.R segments each gene among its targets.  You only have 1 target within each gene and this leads to a bug.

It seems a lot of the genes have similar names — you can either combine them for segmentation (by naming them the same in gene_qc) or use the chromosomal segmentation code for CODEX by default. Another option is to manually construct targets within each gene — we’ve done this before for large genes that are captured in full.

Hope this is of help to you,

Yuchao

messages.subject: Re: [codex_wes_cnv] questions about targeted sequencing results
parts:
Hi Carrie,

I think you might need to experiment on that — sequencing depth among other factors can potentially affect the results if you want to manually create pseudo targets. Also please make sure that your data is from human sample and assembled in hg19 otherwise the default computation for GC content and mappability won’t be correct.

Another way to directly call without segmentation is to get a z-score:

z=log(Y_qc/Yhat[[4]]) # 4 is the optimal number of latent factors that is chosen in this case

Z is then a matrix of number of targets x number of samples. Since you only have one target per gene, you can simply perform a thresholding on each row of z. That is, if the corresponding z score is less than -1 call it a deletion; if it is greater than 1, call it a duplication (the null for z-score is centered at 0).

Hope this helpful,
Yuchao

messages.subject: Re: [codex_wes_cnv] questions about targeted sequencing results
parts:
Thank you so much for all of your help and advice! My data are is from humans and assembled in hg19. When I broke down the genes into multiple targets, it worked perfectly :-)

best,
Carrie
On Sat, Oct 7, 2017 at 1:39 PM, Yuchao Jiang <yj...@cornell.edu> wrote:

Hi Carrie,

I think you might need to experiment on that — sequencing depth among other factors can potentially affect the results if you want to manually create pseudo targets. Also please make sure that your data is from human sample and assembled in hg19 otherwise the default computation for GC content and mappability won’t be correct.

Another way to directly call without segmentation is to get a z-score:

z=log(Y_qc/Yhat[[4]]) # 4 is the optimal number of latent factors that is chosen in this case

Z is then a matrix of number of targets x number of samples. Since you only have one target per gene, you can simply perform a thresholding on each row of z. That is, if the corresponding z score is less than -1 call it a deletion; if it is greater than 1, call it a duplication (the null for z-score is centered at 0).

Hope this helpful,
Yuchao
On Oct 6, 2017, at 10:20 AM, Carrie Veilleux <carrie.c...@gmail.com> wrote:

Thank you so much! I'll try adding more targets within each gene. How many targets (or what size targets) do you recommend? Most of my genes are a single exon, around 900-1100 bp long.

best,
Carrie

On Thu, Oct 5, 2017 at 5:44 PM, Yuchao Jiang <yj...@cornell.edu> wrote:
Hi,

I took a look at your rda file. The error you got was due to the fact that each gene has only 1 target. You have 860 targets after QC, which correspond to 860 genes. The segmentation procedure by segment_targeted.R segments each gene among its targets.  You only have 1 target within each gene and this leads to a bug.

It seems a lot of the genes have similar names — you can either combine them for segmentation (by naming them the same in gene_qc) or use the chromosomal segmentation code for CODEX by default. Another option is to manually construct targets within each gene — we’ve done this before for large genes that are captured in full.

Hope this is of help to you,

Yuchao


On Oct 3, 2017, at 9:04 AM, Carrie Veilleux <carrie.c...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Yuchao,

I was hoping I've just been doing something slightly wrong! The for loop you provided is identical to the one I'm using, so I'm attaching the image rda file.

The only other thing I think I specifically did differently than the targeted sequencing code was that the chromosomes on my .bam files are all labeled with "chr", so I had to specify chr= "chr1", chr= "chr2", etc. rather than chr=1, chr=2.

Thank you so much for all of your help!
Carrie

On Mon, Oct 2, 2017 at 12:57 PM, Yuchao Jiang <yj...@cornell.edu> wrote:
Hi Carrie,

You need to use the segmentation function for targeted sequencing since the targets are very sparse along the genome and segmentation for each chromosome wouldnt make sense. I think there must be something wrong with your code.  Can you try debug by looking into the for loop? This code has been used several times and I feel you might have some trivial misspecification.

for(genei in unique(gene_qc)){
+ cat('Segmenting gene',genei,'\n')
+ geneindex=which(gene_qc==genei)
+ yi=Y_qc[geneindex,]
+ yhati=Yhat[[optK]][geneindex,]
+ refi=ref_qc[geneindex]
+ chri=chr_qc[geneindex][1]
+ finalcalli=segment_targeted(yi, yhati, sampname_qc, refi, genei, chri, lmax=length(geneindex), mode='integer')
+ finalcall=rbind(finalcall,finalcalli)
+ }
 

If you cannot find it, please use save.image(file=‘codex_debug.rda’) and send me the image rda file (or share with me via Google or Dropbox if it is too large). I can help you look into it.

Cheers,
Yuchao



On Oct 2, 2017, at 12:30 PM, Carrie Veilleux <carrie.c...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Yuchao,

Thank you so much for your quick reply!
 
I think your number of latent factors is chosen to high (opt =13 currently). This will remove most of your CNV signals as latent artifacts or batch effects. You can refer to the pdf generated in the choiceofK() step however it can be sometimes not indicative of an optimal value. If this is the case, I still would recommend a smaller optK — we rarely set this value to be greater than 10 in our analysis (usually around 5). Also for your dataset, it seems that you have some positive controls, which you can use to guide the choice of optK (i.e., try different optK and see if the known CNV signals are retained without too many potential false positives).
 
I thought the high K might be a problem too. I have run it with a lower K and when I use the segment_targeted.R for segmentation with a lower K (even K=2, K=5, etc.), the result in finalcall is still one row of NAs when following the targeted sequencing code.

However, if I use the finalcall code in the vignette instead of segment_targeted.R
finalcall <- segment(Y_qc, Yhat, optK = optK, K = K, sampname_qc, ref_qc, chr, lmax = 200, mode = "integer")
I get results in the finalcall file, and the number of deletions/duplications does vary depending on what I set as optK. If I set it at 5, for example, there are 876 deletions/duplications, whereas if I set it optK= 11 there are 422.

Should I use the finalcall code from the vignette instead of the segment_targeted.R even though I have a targeted sequencing dataset? And then try different optK based on the positive controls, as you mentioned above?

Thank you so much!
Carrie
